title: Telling Luck From Cause in Populations
endLine: Model random mating and chance drift to tell luck from cause.

scenes.tts: When one version of a gene grows common, did selection favour it, or did plain luck? Population-genetic models first predict what chance alone would do.
scenes.caption: When one version of a gene grows common, did selection favour it, or did plain luck? Population-genetic models first predict what chance alone would do.
scenes.visual: Schematic: a large pool of amber and teal beads fills the left side beside a vertical frequency track from zero to 1. Amber beads grow more common across generations as a bright trace climbs the track; the bright label 'Selection or luck?' appears above the rising curve.
scenes.narration: When one version of a gene grows common, did selection favour it, or did plain luck? Population-genetic models first predict what chance alone would do.

scenes.visual: The amber and teal beads drift slowly in the background as the title 'Telling Luck From Cause in Populations' appears cleanly in the center, then fades back to the bead pool.

scenes.tts: At one locus, a place on a chromosome, a population carries gene versions called alleles. Two alleles, big A and little a, have allele frequencies p and q. Together, p plus q equals one.
scenes.caption: At one locus, a place on a chromosome, a population carries gene versions called alleles. Two alleles, A and a, have allele frequencies p and q. Together, p + q = 1.
scenes.visual: Schematic: the bead pool resolves into mating individuals carrying two bead slots at one highlighted locus, labelled 'A' in amber and 'a' in teal. A full-width bar splits into amber segment 'p' and teal segment 'q', labelled 'p + q = 1'.
scenes.narration: At one locus, a place on a chromosome, a population carries gene versions called alleles. Two alleles, A and a, have allele frequencies p and q. Together, p + q = 1.

scenes.tts: For Hardy-Weinberg proportions, suppose a large population mates randomly, with no selection, mutation, or migration. Eggs and sperm pair by chance, so multiply their frequencies for each genotype, or allele pair. Big A big A is p times p; little a little a is q times q. Big A little a forms both ways: p times q plus q times p.
scenes.caption: For Hardy-Weinberg proportions, suppose a large population mates randomly, with no selection, mutation, or migration. Eggs and sperm pair by chance, so multiply their frequencies for each genotype, or allele pair. AA is p × p; aa is q × q. Aa forms both ways: p × q + q × p.
scenes.visual: Schematic: the 'p' and 'q' bar copies onto the top (sperm) and left (eggs) sides of a large square filling the frame. Four tiles light up as named: amber 'AA = p × p', teal 'aa = q × q', and two striped amber-teal tiles 'Aa = p × q' and 'Aa = q × p', labelled 'Hardy-Weinberg proportions'.
scenes.narration: For Hardy-Weinberg proportions, suppose a large population mates randomly, with no selection, mutation, or migration. Eggs and sperm pair by chance, so multiply their frequencies for each genotype, or allele pair. AA is p × p; aa is q × q. Aa forms both ways: p × q + q × p.

scenes.tts: Recount big A. Big A big A is all A: p times p. The two big A little a tiles total two p q; half their copies are A, giving p q. That sums to p times, p plus q. Since p plus q equals one, that stays p. Mating reshuffles alleles without changing their frequency.
scenes.caption: Recount A. AA is all A: p × p. The two Aa tiles total 2pq; half their copies are A, giving pq. That sums to p × (p + q). Since p + q = 1, that stays p. Mating reshuffles alleles without changing their frequency.
scenes.visual: Schematic: inside the same square, 'aa' dims while 'AA' glows full amber ('all A', 'p × p'). The two 'Aa' tiles join and show '2pq', then split in half vertically ('half A' → 'pq') as spoken. The amber 'AA' tile and the amber halves slide together into one amber strip labelled 'p × p + p × q', which refolds into 'p × (p + q)'; '(p + q)' turns to '1' and the strip aligns to width 'p' along the 'p + q = 1' edge.
scenes.narration: Recount A. AA is all A: p × p. The two Aa tiles total 2pq; half their copies are A, giving pq. That sums to p × (p + q). Since p + q = 1, that stays p. Mating reshuffles alleles without changing their frequency.

scenes.tts: In a small population, chance sampling moves allele frequencies: that is genetic drift. Two chance steps drive it: which parental copy enters each egg or sperm, and how many offspring each parent leaves. Drift needs no difference in fitness, the relative number of surviving offspring. So harmful alleles can rise, or beneficial ones vanish.
scenes.caption: In a small population, chance sampling moves allele frequencies: that is genetic drift. Two chance steps drive it: which parental copy enters each egg or sperm, and how many offspring each parent leaves. Drift needs no difference in fitness, the relative number of surviving offspring. So harmful alleles can rise, or beneficial ones vanish.
scenes.visual: Schematic: the large square shrinks into a small bead bag holding a handful of amber and teal beads. Random draws pick one of each parent's two beads and vary each parent's offspring count; the frequency dot on the zero to 1 track lurches up and down, labelled 'Genetic drift'.
scenes.narration: In a small population, chance sampling moves allele frequencies: that is genetic drift. Two chance steps drive it: which parental copy enters each egg or sperm, and how many offspring each parent leaves. Drift needs no difference in fitness, the relative number of surviving offspring. So harmful alleles can rise, or beneficial ones vanish.

scenes.tts: Now start replicate populations at the same frequency and keep them alike. Let only chance act for many generations. What happens to the spread among replicates, and to their average?
scenes.caption: Now start replicate populations at the same frequency and keep them alike. Let only chance act for many generations. What happens to the spread among replicates, and to their average?
scenes.visual: Schematic: the small bead bag duplicates into several identical small pools aligned at the same starting mark on the zero to 1 frequency track. Their frequency dots wait at the starting line as the bright question 'Spread? Average?' appears above.
scenes.narration: Now start replicate populations at the same frequency and keep them alike. Let only chance act for many generations. What happens to the spread among replicates, and to their average?

scenes.visual: Schematic: keep the aligned replicate bead pools and the 'Spread? Average?' question on screen during the pause while the beads inside each pool shimmer gently.

scenes.tts: Across replicates, drift spreads allele frequencies apart without pushing their average. Chance favours no allele, so the expected average stays put. That is the neutral null: what chance alone predicts. Consistent selection or gene flow from immigrants pushes the average.
scenes.caption: Across replicates, drift spreads allele frequencies apart without pushing their average. Chance favours no allele, so the expected average stays put. That is the neutral null: what chance alone predicts. Consistent selection or gene flow from immigrants pushes the average.
scenes.visual: Schematic: the replicate lines release across generations on the zero to 1 track, fanning wide while a bold white average line wobbles gently near the start ('Neutral null'). A contrasting bundle then shifts upward together with its average line ('Selection or gene flow').
scenes.narration: Across replicates, drift spreads allele frequencies apart without pushing their average. Chance favours no allele, so the expected average stays put. That is the neutral null: what chance alone predicts. Consistent selection or gene flow from immigrants pushes the average.

scenes.tts: One trap: a single population's frequency cannot tell luck from cause, since drift and selection both move it. So compare the replicates' average with the neutral null. Test selection with a fitness assay, and gene flow with ancestry.
scenes.caption: One trap: a single population's frequency cannot tell luck from cause, since drift and selection both move it. So compare the replicates' average with the neutral null. Test selection with a fitness assay, and gene flow with ancestry.
scenes.visual: Schematic: all replicate traces fade except one rising line labelled 'One population: luck or cause?', with two faint arrows behind it tagged 'drift' and 'selection'. All traces return with their average line beside the dashed 'Neutral null'. Three crisp check badges appear in order as spoken beside the track: 'Average vs neutral null', 'Fitness assay', and 'Ancestry'.
scenes.narration: One trap: a single population's frequency cannot tell luck from cause, since drift and selection both move it. So compare the replicates' average with the neutral null. Test selection with a fitness assay, and gene flow with ancestry.

scenes.tts: In conservation, genes can help a small population too. In 1995, managers released eight female pumas from Texas into southern Florida's small, inbred panther population. By 2010, panther numbers had about tripled, and heterozygosity, a measure of genetic variation, had doubled.
scenes.caption: In conservation, genes can help a small population too. In 1995, managers released eight female pumas from Texas into southern Florida's small, inbred panther population. By 2010, panther numbers had about tripled, and heterozygosity, a measure of genetic variation, had doubled.
scenes.visual: Schematic: the bead pool morphs into a small, nearly uniform dot cluster in southern Florida ('Florida panthers'), joined by eight contrasting arcs arriving from Texas ('1995: eight Texas pumas'). Beside it, two rising bars animate to 2010: 'Numbers: about tripled' and 'Heterozygosity: doubled'.
scenes.narration: In conservation, genes can help a small population too. In 1995, managers released eight female pumas from Texas into southern Florida's small, inbred panther population. By 2010, panther numbers had about tripled, and heterozygosity, a measure of genetic variation, had doubled.

scenes.tts: In 2010, Hugo Snippert, Clevers and colleagues asked: does each division make one stem cell and one short-lived progenitor? They gave mouse small-intestinal stem cells one of four colours. Most divisions were symmetric. Over 1 to 6 months, some colour patches, each one cell's descendants, grew while others vanished. That fits stem-cell positions won or lost by chance: neutral drift.
scenes.caption: In 2010, Hugo Snippert, Clevers and colleagues asked: does each division make one stem cell and one short-lived progenitor? scenes.visual: Schematic: the dot cluster becomes a ring of small-intestinal stem cells tagged '2010: Snippert, Clevers and colleagues'. A small diagram of the tested rule ('one stem cell + one short-lived progenitor') appears and is crossed out as 'Most divisions were symmetric' is spoken. Cells take one of four bright colours; across '1 to 6 months', some single-colour patches (clones) expand around the ring while others vanish, as faint neutral-drift replicate traces re-emerge behind the ring.
scenes.narration: In 2010, Hugo Snippert, Clevers and colleagues asked: does each division make one stem cell and one short-lived progenitor? They gave mouse small-intestinal stem cells one of four colours. Most divisions were symmetric. Over 1 to 6 months, some colour patches, each one cell's descendants, grew while others vanished. That fits stem-cell positions won or lost by chance: neutral drift.

scenes.visual: The ring and drift traces fade to a clean dark frame, leaving the bright centered end-card rule: 'Model random mating and chance drift to tell luck from cause.'
